extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, historians of economic thought, and policymakers interested in coinage and colonial policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and policy-relevant criteria from a chapter of a political-economy treatise (discussion of coinage/seignorage and motives for colonies). Useful for policy comment, historical analysis, or regulatory notice-and-comment grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullion as the most convenient instrument for round‑about foreign trade
rubrics_metrics.description: “A round-about foreign trade of consumption can be carried on more advantageously by means of these metals than of almost any other goods. As they are the universal instruments of commerce, they are more readily received in return for all commodities than any other goods; and, on account of their small bulk and great value, it costs less to transport them backward and forward ... and they lose less of their value by being so transported.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Gold and silver are singled out as the most convenient commodities to use in multi‑stage (round‑about) foreign trade because of universal acceptability and low transport costs per value. Implication for policy/valuation: when assessing the value of a trading relationship or a colony, consider the role of bullion in facilitating exchanges where direct commodity-for-commodity trade is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seignorage as a preventive against melting and exportation of coin
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wherever money is received by tale, therefore, a seignorage is the most effectual preventive of the melting down of the coin, and, for the same reason, of its exportation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Charging a coinage duty (seignorage) raises the market value of coin relative to bullion sufficiently to remove the profit from melting or exporting high-quality coin. Practical example in text: when coin was degenerated, melting new coin produced bullion sellable at >mint price, creating profit; a seignorage large enough could eliminate that profit and thus stop the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of seignorage size to profit/loss from melting new coin
rubrics_metrics.description: “This profit always arises from the difference between the quantity of bullion which the common currency ought to contain and that which it actually does contain. If this difference is less than the seignorage, there will be loss instead of profit. If it is equal to the seignorage, there will be neither profit nor loss. If it is greater than the seignorage, there will ... some profit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance with numeric illustrations: the chapter gives hypothetical percentages (e.g., coin 2% underweight; seignorage examples of 1%, 2%, 5%) to show how differing seignorage rates change whether melting is profitable. Use this test: compare the percentage deficiency of circulating coin vs. seignorage percentage to predict incentives to melt or export coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate seignorage does not raise final cost because money has no last consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the tax upon a commodity is so moderate as not to encourage smuggling, the merchant who deals in it, though he advances, does not properly pay the tax, as he gets it back in the price of the commodity. The tax is finally paid by the last purchaser or consumer. But money is a commodity, with regard to which every man is a merchant... When the tax upon coinage, therefore, is so moderate as not to encourage false coining, though every body advances the tax, nobody finally pays it; because every body gets it back in the advanced value of the coin.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: A moderate coinage duty, below the threshold that encourages counterfeiting/smuggling, will not effectively increase the cost borne by any final consumer because every holder trades money onward. Thus concerns that modest seignorage unfairly burdens banks/merchants are misplaced if it stays moderate.

rubrics_metrics.name: If coin contains full standard weight, coinage costs nothing to anybody
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whether there is or is not a seignorage, if the currency contains its full standard weight, the coinage costs nothing to anybody; and if it is short of that weight, the coinage must always cost the difference between the quantity of bullion which ought to be contained in it, and that which actually is contained in it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Evaluate coinage policy by assessing actual coin quality relative to standard weight. If currency is at full standard, removing seignorage or charging it yields no net cost (aside from administrative fees); if currency is degraded, the shortfall determines the cost that will be borne by those who coin bullion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exorbitant seignorage can encourage counterfeiting, but severity of penalties matters
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the duty was exorbitant, indeed, ... false coiners ... might be encouraged, by the great difference between the value of bullion and that of coin, to pour in so great a quantity of counterfeit money as might reduce the value of the government money. In France, however, though the seignorage is eight per cent., no sensible inconveniency of this kind is found to arise from it. The dangers to which a false coiner is everywhere exposed ... are by far too great to be incurred for the sake of a profit of six or seven per cent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance required: while high seignorage increases incentives for counterfeiting, strong detection and punishment (or other disincentives) can prevent it; empirical observation (France) shows moderately high seignorage need not produce counterfeiting if risks are severe. Use both rate-setting and enforcement when designing coinage duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government paying coinage is gratuitous and forfeits small revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: “The government, therefore, when it defrays the expense of coinage, not only incurs some small expense, but loses some small revenue which it might get by a proper duty; and neither the bank, nor any other private persons, are in the smallest degree benefited by this useless piece of public generosity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy takeaway: Making coinage duty-free is effectively a transfer from the public revenue to private parties (bank or bullion holders) without social benefit. Governments should weigh the small revenue foregone against political or administrative considerations when deciding to defray coinage costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank/merchant incentives in relation to coinage practice and weighing custom
rubrics_metrics.description: “The bank of England ... are frequently obliged to carry bullion to the mint; and it was more for their interest, they probably imagined, that the coinage should be at the expense of the government than at their own. ... Should the custom of weighing gold, however, come to be disused ... this great company may, perhaps, find that they have ... mistaken their own interest not a little.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational criterion: the institutional practice (e.g., whether gold is accepted by weight or by tale) affects private incentives. Changes in transactional custom can shift whether banks benefit from government-paid coinage; analysts should assess institutional practices before judging who benefits from coinage subsidies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial motives differ by historical context (Greek, Roman, modern European)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The interest which occasioned the first settlement of the different European colonies in America and the West Indies, was not altogether so plain and distinct as that which directed the establishment of those of ancient Greece and Rome. ... The colonies of the Dorians ... The Roman colonies ... were at all times subject to the correction, jurisdiction, and legislative authority of the mother city.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical criterion: when evaluating colonies or colonial policy, distinguish the motivating interests (population pressure, land distribution, military garrisoning, commercial/imperial motives). The text lays out different institutional forms and motives that shape outcomes — useful as a typology for evaluating colonial projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: European colonization driven largely by search for precious metals, not evident utility
rubrics_metrics.description: “The establishment of the European colonies in America and the West Indies arose from no necessity; and though the utility which has resulted from them has been very great, it is not altogether so clear and evident. It was not understood at their first establishment ... It was the sacred thirst of gold that carried Ovieda ... Cortes to Mexico, Almagro and Pizarro to Chili and Peru.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the justification or motives for colonial ventures, prioritize the economic incentives (search for gold/silver) rather than later rationalizations (civilizing missions, conversion). Policy and moral evaluation should account for primary economic drivers and their consequences (e.g., exploitation, instability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy taxation can destroy mining incentives and reduce production
rubrics_metrics.description: “As long as the whole, or the greater part of the gold which the first adventurers imported into Europe was got by so very easy a method ... it was not perhaps very difficult to pay even this heavy tax; but when the natives were once fairly stript ... and when, in order to find more, it had become necessary to dig for it in the mines, there was no longer any possibility of paying this tax. The rigorous exaction of it, accordingly, first occasioned ... the total abandoning of the mines of St. Domingo ... It was soon reduced, therefore, to a third; then to a fifth; afterwards to a tenth; and at last to a twentieth part of the gross produce of the gold mines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical lesson: extremely high taxation of extractive rents can lead to abandonment of resource exploitation. Use this historical sequence to argue that tax schedules should be calibrated to sustain productive activity; consider reduction or restructuring of tax burdens if they impede extraction and long‑term revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for new mines is an unwise target for extraordinary encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all those expensive and uncertain projects ... there is none, perhaps, more perfectly ruinous than the search after new silver and gold mines. It is, perhaps, the most disadvantageous lottery in the world ... Projects of mining, instead of replacing the capital employed in them, together with the ordinary profits of stock, commonly absorb both capital and profit. ... a prudent lawgiver, who desired to increase the capital of his nation, would least choose to give any extraordinary encouragement ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendation: Governments should be cautious about subsidizing or otherwise giving extraordinary encouragement to speculative mining projects because the social return is generally low and the private losses large. This can inform cost‑benefit analysis of incentives for extractive industries.
